title: Delta in Cassiopeia
html_source:
This phrase is recurs at several points in the novel. It is first seen back in Proteus (“Darkly they are there behind this light, darkness shining in the brightness, delta of Cassiopeia”).

When Shakespeare was 8 years old, a bright light appeared in the sky in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was a supernova explosion, but most people (including Tycho Brahe) took it to be a new star forming. (Indeed, Brahe published a tract called “Concerning the Star, new and never before seen in the life or memory of anyone.”) It is one of only 8 supernovae witnessed in recorded history and caused much ado in Elizabethan England. Many took it to be a sign of the second coming of Christ. The brightness grew and grew relative to other objects in the night sky, only to disappear altogether after 16 months (when Shakespeare would have been 9).

For more on Cassiopeia in Ulysses (including later mentions and thus spoilers), see this blog post.
